turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I want to do a day hike on Sunday but I'm not super fit.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No problem. There's a flat lakeside loop of about five miles, or a shorter trail with a steep climb and a great view. Which appeals more?

contexts.pending: flat lakeside loop or short steep trail with a view
think_reask: So, the flat loop around the lake, or the steep one with the view?
Okay, time's up. Lakeside loop or the short climb?
welcome_back: Welcome back. You were choosing a hike for Sunday, the lake loop or the steep trail?
Hi again. Did you pick between the flat walk and the climb with the view?

endings.user: The lake. I'd rather enjoy it than suffer.
endings.moshi: Good choice. Bring a picnic, there are benches along the shore.

endings.user: The steep one. I want the view, even if I'm slow.
endings.moshi: Go for it. Take plenty of breaks and start early before it gets hot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My old boots finally fell apart.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Time for new ones. Do you want proper leather boots with ankle support, or lighter trail shoes?

contexts.pending: leather boots with ankle support or light trail shoes
think_reask: So, sturdy leather boots, or lighter trail shoes?
Have you decided? Ankle support or something lighter?
welcome_back: Welcome back. We were picking new hiking footwear, boots or trail shoes?
There you are. Still deciding between boots and trail shoes?

endings.user: Boots. I twisted my ankle last year and I don't want that again.
endings.moshi: Makes sense. Break them in on short walks before any big hike.

endings.user: Trail shoes. I mostly do easy paths in summer.
endings.moshi: Then they'll be much more comfortable. Pick a pair with a good grippy sole.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friends invited me on a hike but the forecast says rain in the afternoon.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Tricky. You could start very early and be down before the rain, or move the hike to another day. What do you think?

contexts.pending: start early before the rain or postpone the hike
think_reask: So, an early start to beat the rain, or postpone it?
Okay, what's the plan, go early or pick another day?
welcome_back: Welcome back. You were deciding about the hike and the rain. Early start or postpone?
Hi again. Any decision on the rainy hike?

endings.user: Let's go early. Everyone's already free that day.
endings.moshi: Then aim to be on the trail by seven, and still pack a rain jacket just in case.

endings.user: Postpone. Muddy trails are no fun.
endings.moshi: Fair. Next weekend looks drier, so suggest that to the group.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My wife's just had knee surgery and she's itching to get back on the trails.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good for her. The old railway path is completely flat but a bit dull, while the marsh boardwalk is prettier with a few steps. Which would she rather start with?

contexts.pending: railway path or marsh boardwalk for a post-surgery walk
think_reask: So for her first walk back, the flat railway path or the boardwalk with the steps?
Which one feels right for her knee, the railway path or the marsh?
welcome_back: Back to your wife's comeback walk. Railway path or marsh boardwalk?
For her knee, were you leaning towards the dead flat path or the prettier boardwalk?

endings.user: The railway path. Boring is fine for now, she'll just be happy to be out.
endings.moshi: Sensible. Let her set the pace, and turn around before she feels she has to.

endings.user: She'd hate the boring one. Let's do the boardwalk and take the steps slowly.
endings.moshi: Fair enough. A short loop with a bench halfway would be ideal, then.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I really want to see a sunrise from the top of Pike Hill.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That means starting in the dark with a head torch, around half past four. Or you could go up for sunset and come down in the dusk. Are you a morning person?

contexts.pending: sunrise start in the dark or sunset hike
think_reask: Right then, half past four with a head torch, or the sunset version?
Have you made peace with the early alarm, or is it sunset after all?
welcome_back: So, about Pike Hill. Sunrise in the dark, or sunset instead?
You were weighing a four thirty alarm against an evening climb. Any closer?

endings.user: Sunrise. If I don't do it now I never will.
endings.moshi: Love it. Lay everything out the night before so you're not hunting for socks at four.

endings.user: Honestly, sunset. I'm useless before seven.
endings.moshi: No shame in that. Just make sure your torch is charged for the walk down.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, trekking poles. My knees are begging me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Smart move. Cheap aluminium ones are tough but bulky, and carbon folding ones pack tiny but cost about three times as much.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ugh, money.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: So how often would you actually use them, every weekend or a few times a year?

contexts.pending: cheap aluminium poles or pricier carbon folding poles
think_reask: So, aluminium and save the cash, or splash out on the folding carbon ones?
Every weekend or a few times a year? That decides the poles.
welcome_back: Back to your knees. Bulky aluminium poles or the little folding carbon ones?
The poles question is still open. Cheap and sturdy, or light and expensive?

endings.user: Most weekends, if I'm honest. I'll get the carbon ones.
endings.moshi: Then they'll pay for themselves. Set them a bit shorter for the uphill bits.

endings.user: A few times a year. Aluminium is plenty.
endings.moshi: Good call. They'll last for ages, and you can always upgrade later.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've organised a team hike for work and one guy is really, really slow.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That happens. You could split into a fast and a slow group with a meeting point, or keep everyone together at his pace. How would he feel about being split off?

contexts.pending: split the work group or keep everyone together
think_reask: So for the team hike, two groups or everyone at one pace?
Have you decided how to handle the slow walker? Split or stick together?
welcome_back: About your work hike. Split the group, or keep everyone together?
We'd got to the slow colleague. Two groups with a meeting point, or one group?

endings.user: Together. It's meant to be team building, not a race.
endings.moshi: Agreed. Put him near the front, it stops the gap from opening up.

endings.user: Split it, but I'll walk with the slow group myself.
endings.moshi: That's kind. Pick a meeting point with a view, so nobody minds waiting.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We want to take our little girl hiking. She's two and a half.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fun age. You could carry her in a hiking backpack and do a proper route, or let her toddle a tiny trail with lots of puddles. Which sounds more like your family?

contexts.pending: carry the toddler on a proper route or let her walk a tiny trail
think_reask: So, toddler in the backpack on a real route, or her own little puddle trail?
Carrier and a proper hike, or a short walk at her speed?
welcome_back: Your little hiker. Backpack carrier, or let her walk a tiny trail?
So for the two and a half year old, proper route in the carrier or a puddle trail?

endings.user: Let her walk. She'll be furious if she can't jump in puddles.
endings.moshi: Then keep it under a mile and pack spare trousers. Lots of them.

endings.user: The carrier. We miss proper hikes.
endings.moshi: Fair. Stop every hour so she can run around, or she'll get grumpy up there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: It's going to be thirty five degrees tomorrow and I'm supposed to do the canyon trail.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's brutal heat with no shade. You could start at dawn and be out by ten, or swap to the shady forest trail. Which would you prefer?

contexts.pending: canyon at dawn or the shady forest trail in the heat
think_reask: So, canyon at the crack of dawn, or the forest where it's cooler?
Dawn start in the canyon or switch to the shade? Your call.
welcome_back: About tomorrow's heat. Early canyon, or the forest trail?
The canyon in thirty five degrees. Going at dawn, or swapping?

endings.user: Forest. I'm not risking heatstroke for a photo.
endings.moshi: Wise. Still take extra water, forests get humid in a heatwave.

endings.user: Dawn canyon. I've waited months for this one.
endings.moshi: Okay, then be off the trail by ten, and carry at least three litres.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I moved here in spring and I still haven't found anyone to hike with.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That can be lonely. There's a local rambling club with a small yearly fee, or a free app where people post group walks. Would you prefer regular faces or more flexibility?

contexts.pending: join the rambling club or use the group walk app
think_reask: So, the rambling club with regulars, or the app and see who turns up?
Regular faces or flexibility? Which way are you leaning?
welcome_back: Finding hiking company. The club, or the app?
Back to meeting people out here. Rambling club or the walk app?

endings.user: The club. I want to see the same people and actually make friends.
endings.moshi: Good thinking. Go to three walks before you judge it, the first one's always awkward.

endings.user: The app for now. I'm not ready to commit to a club.
endings.moshi: Makes sense. Try a few different groups and see who you click with.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: For Saturday's walk, do I pack lunch?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Depends. The route passes a mountain hut that's famous for its soup, but it closes at two. A packed lunch means you can stop anywhere. Fancy the gamble on timing?

contexts.pending: pack lunch or aim for the mountain hut soup
think_reask: So, sandwiches in the bag, or race the clock for that soup?
Packed lunch or the hut before two?
welcome_back: Saturday's lunch. Hut soup or your own sandwiches?
So, are you chasing the soup before it closes, or packing your own?

endings.user: Soup. I'll set off early so we make it.
endings.moshi: Good plan. Throw a cereal bar in anyway, just in case you're late.

endings.user: I'll pack lunch. I don't want to rush the views.
endings.moshi: Fair. Eat it at the top, then you can grab a hot drink at the hut if it's open.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep getting a bit lost on hikes. Nothing dramatic, just wrong turns.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Happens to everyone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I just buy a GPS watch?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You could, or take a one day map and compass course so you never depend on batteries. Gadget or skill, which suits you?

contexts.pending: buy a GPS watch or take a map and compass course
think_reask: So, the GPS watch, or learn the map and compass?
Gadget or skill? Which one are you going for?
welcome_back: About those wrong turns. Watch or navigation course?
The getting lost problem. GPS watch, or a map and compass day?

endings.user: The course. I like the idea of not needing a screen.
endings.moshi: Great. You'll start noticing the land around you much more, too.

endings.user: Watch. I'm never going to fold a map in the wind.
endings.moshi: Fair enough. Just keep a spare charge for it on longer days.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: {friend}, have you seen my water bottle? The big green one.

turns.speaker: friend
turns.text: It's in the car from last weekend, I think.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ugh, it's probably gross by now.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Thanks. Do you want to come with us tomorrow, by the way?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Would it be okay for the kids?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should I pack for a day hike? It's my first one.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: The basics are water, snacks, a light rain jacket, sunscreen and a charged phone. A small first aid kit is a good idea too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How much water are we talking?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: About half a litre per hour of hiking, more if it's hot. For a four hour walk, two litres is a safe amount.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's heavy. Can I / just bring one bottle and refill it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Only if you know there's safe water along the way. Streams aren't safe to drink without a filter.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, two litres it is. What kind of snacks?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Things that are easy to eat on the move, like nuts, dried fruit, cereal bars or a sandwich. Salty snacks are nice if you sweat a lot.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I keep getting blisters on my heels when I hike.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's usually friction from your heel sliding in the boot. Are your boots well broken in?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They're pretty new, yeah.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's likely the cause. Wear them around the house and on short walks first. Proper hiking socks help a lot too, not cotton ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if I feel one starting on the trail?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Stop right away and put a blister plaster or some tape on the spot. Waiting until it hurts usually means it's already formed.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I always think I'll / just push through it.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most people do. A two minute stop early saves you a miserable walk back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is it safe to hike alone?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be, with some precautions. Pick a well used trail, and always tell someone where you're going and when you'll be back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I get lost?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Download an offline map before you go and carry a small battery pack for your phone. If you're unsure, stay where you are and call for help.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm retired, so I can go on weekdays when it's / really quiet.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's lovely, but quieter trails mean fewer people to help. Stick to routes you know until you're confident.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good point. Maybe I'll join a walking group too.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a great idea. Many groups do weekday hikes, and you'll learn new trails from them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can I take my dog on a long hike?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most healthy adult dogs love it. How old is your dog, and what breed?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She's a three year old border collie.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect, collies have tons of energy. She'll probably outlast you. Just build up the distance gradually.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What does she need to bring?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Water and a collapsible bowl, some treats, and poo bags. Check her paws during breaks, rocky trails can hurt them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I / keep her on the lead the whole time?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the trail rules first. Near livestock or wildlife, a lead is always the safer choice.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I got a pounding headache near the top of the mountain yesterday. Is that normal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: How high were you? Above about two and a half thousand metres, a headache can be a mild sign of altitude sickness.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Just under three thousand, I think.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then that's quite likely. Did it get better once you came down?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Yeah, pretty much straight away. I'd / also barely had any water, to be fair.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Dehydration makes it much worse. Next time, drink steadily on the way up, go a bit slower, and if the headache grows or you feel sick, head down.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So going down is basically the cure?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: For mild symptoms, yes. Descending even a few hundred metres usually helps quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a field full of cows on the footpath I want to use. Am I being silly to be scared?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not silly at all. Cows are usually calm, but mothers with calves can get protective.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh great. So what do I do?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Walk calmly around the edge of the herd rather than through the middle, and don't get between a cow and her calf.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they start following me?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep walking steadily, don't run. If you have a dog and they come at you, let the dog off the lead, it can outrun them and they'll chase it instead of you.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't have a dog. Just a / very nervous husband.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then hold hands and stroll along the hedge. Most of the time, they'll just stare.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm sixteen and my friends think hiking is boring. How do I get them to come?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pick a route with a payoff they'll care about, like a swimming spot, a rope swing, or a crazy view for photos.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a lake with a jetty you can jump off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. Sell it as a lake day that happens to need a walk to get there.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, sneaky. How long should it be?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep it short the first time, maybe an hour each way. If they enjoy it, they'll be up for longer ones.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And food?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Bring something good to share at the lake. Nobody complains about a hike that ends with crisps and a jump into cold water.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Going uphill is fine, but my knees kill me on the way down.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's really common. Downhill puts a lot more load on the front of the knee.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Is there a trick?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Take shorter steps, keep your knees slightly bent, and don't lock them. Zigzagging on wide paths helps too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend swears by poles.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: She's right. Poles take a good chunk of the strain off your knees on steep descents. Lengthen them a bit before you head down.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay. And should I / be doing exercises at home?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, squats and step downs off a stair build the muscles that protect your knees. A few minutes a day makes a difference within weeks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Quick one. Is it okay to throw an orange peel into the bushes? It's natural, right?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It feels harmless, but it's better to take it home. Peel takes a long time to break down, sometimes months or more.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Seriously? Months?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, especially in dry or cold places. And it's not part of what animals there would normally eat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Huh. Same with apple cores?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Same idea. On busy trails, hundreds of people dropping cores adds up quickly.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Fine, I'll / bring a little bag for scraps.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's all it takes. A small zip bag in the side pocket and you're sorted.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm doing a hike in October and it'll be chilly in the morning but warm by lunch. What do I wear?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Layers are your friend. A thin base layer that wicks sweat, a fleece or light jumper on top, and a windproof or waterproof jacket in your bag.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No cotton t-shirt?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Best avoided. Cotton holds sweat and gets cold when you stop for a break.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I hate stopping to change, though. It's so / faffy.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try to take a layer off just before you start getting hot, rather than after you're sweating. It saves you being cold at the top.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And a hat?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A light beanie and thin gloves are worth the space. Cold hands at the summit ruin a good sandwich.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Can you explain contour lines to me like I'm five?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Imagine you walk around a hill without ever going up or down. The path you'd make is one contour line.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Now do the same thing a bit higher, and again higher. Those rings, drawn from above, are all the contour lines.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So lots of lines squashed together means it's steep?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. You go up a lot in a short distance. Lines far apart mean it's gentle.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, that actually makes sense. And how do I tell / if it's a hill or a hole?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look at the height numbers printed on the lines. If they get bigger towards the middle, it's a hill.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I have asthma, mostly under control. Any tips for hiking with it?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Plenty of people with asthma hike happily. The main thing is always carrying your reliever inhaler where you can reach it, not buried in the bag.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Cold air sets mine off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A buff or scarf over your mouth on cold mornings warms the air a bit. Start slowly to let your lungs adjust.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about pollen? Spring is / pretty bad for me.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the pollen forecast and pick days after rain, or routes higher up and by the coast, where counts are often lower.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good idea. I'll talk to my nurse before the big one in May.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a great plan. She might suggest using your preventer more regularly in the weeks before.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I signed up for a twenty mile charity hike in six weeks. I currently do zero hiking. Help.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Very doable if you start now. Walk three or four times a week, with one longer walk at the weekend that grows each time.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How long should the first long one be?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Maybe six miles. Add two or three miles each week, so you hit about fifteen two weeks before the event.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Not twenty?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: No need. Fifteen plus the adrenaline on the day will carry you. Rest the last week so your legs are fresh.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And I should wear the / exact shoes I'll use on the day?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, in every training walk. Never try new shoes or socks on the big day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What do the little painted marks on trees mean? Some are white, some are yellow.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: They're called blazes, or waymarks. Each colour usually marks a different trail, so you follow one colour from start to finish.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And when there are two stacked on top of each other?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That usually means a turn is coming. If the top mark is offset to one side, the trail turns that way.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, clever. I always thought / someone was just bored with a paint can.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Ha, no, volunteers maintain most of them. If you go a long way without seeing one, you've probably missed a turn, so head back to the last one.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Good to know. That's exactly what happened to me last month.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Most of us have done it. Looking behind you now and then helps too, the marks are often painted on both sides.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My leather boots are ten years old and starting to let water in.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good leather boots can often be revived. Have you waxed or treated them recently?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Never. Not once.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then that's probably it. Clean them with a brush and water, let them dry naturally, then rub in a proper boot wax.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: On the radiator to dry?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Please don't. Heat cracks the leather. Stuff them with newspaper and leave them somewhere airy.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they still leak?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the seams and the sole. If the sole is coming away, a cobbler can often resole them for less than new boots.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I take terrible photos on hikes. Everything looks flat.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's often the light. Midday sun flattens everything. Early morning or late afternoon gives you shadows and warmer colours.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I can't always hike at those times.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Fair. Then try putting something in the foreground, like a rock, a tree or your friend, with the view behind. It adds depth straight away.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, like a person looking out at the view?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly, it also shows how big the landscape is. Just don't make them stand near a cliff edge for it.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Ha, noted. And / should I bother with a proper camera?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Your phone is plenty to start. Learn the basics on that first.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My partner wants to do a full moon night hike. Is that a terrible idea?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not terrible, it can be magical. Just pick a trail you both know well in daylight.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: We've walked the forest loop loads of times, so / that one probably.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good choice. Bring head torches even if the moon is bright, clouds can roll in fast.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Red light or normal?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Red keeps your night vision better for walking under the moon. Switch to white for anything tricky, like rocky steps.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And it gets cold, I guess.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Much colder than you'd expect. Take a warm layer and a hot drink, and tell someone your plan and when you'll be back.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Midges. Last summer they ate me alive by the loch. What actually works?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Repellents with picaridin or a high strength of DEET work best. Some people swear by a head net too, it looks silly but it's bliss.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'll look silly, I don't care.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's the spirit. Midges are worst at dawn and dusk and on still days, so a breezy ridge is much better than a sheltered glen.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And when I stop for lunch?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Find a spot in the wind or the sun. They hate both.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything for the bites themselves? I scratched / until they bled.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: An antihistamine and a cold compress help. Try hard not to scratch, it only makes them itch longer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What should I do if a thunderstorm catches me on a ridge?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Get off the high ground as fast as you safely can. Ridges and summits are the worst places to be.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What if I can't get down in time?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Avoid lone trees and metal fences, and spread out if you're in a group. Crouch low on your pack, feet together, rather than lying flat.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why not lie down?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lying flat puts more of your body in contact with the ground, where current can travel. Crouching keeps that smaller.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Scary stuff.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It is, but rare if you plan well. Check the forecast, and if storms are likely in the afternoon, be off the tops by lunchtime.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I'm five months pregnant. Can I still go hiking?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Many people do, but please check with your midwife or doctor first, since they know your situation.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She said gentle walks are fine. I'm just / not sure what counts as gentle.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Think trails you could chat on without getting breathless, with good footing and not too far from the car or a road.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My balance feels a bit off already.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's very normal as your centre of gravity shifts. Poles help a lot, and avoid loose scree or slippery rocks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And snacks, I guess. I'm starving all the time.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely. Pack more food and water than usual, and take plenty of breaks. You're hiking for two, after all.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I don't drive. Can I still do proper hikes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Absolutely. Linear walks are great for that, you take a bus or train to the start and catch another one home from the end.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Oh, I'd never thought of walking from one station to another.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of good routes work that way, and you never have to walk back the same path.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: But what if I miss the last bus?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Check the timetable before you set off and plan to arrive with an hour to spare. Save a local taxi number as a backup.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Smart. Any / tips for finding these routes?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Rambling clubs and walking guidebooks often list public transport routes. Search for car free walks too.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There's a famous ridge walk my friends want to do, but I'm scared of heights.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a real concern. Do you know how narrow it gets? Some ridges look scary in photos but feel wide when you're on them.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My friend said there's one bit with drops on both sides.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's usually the hardest part for people with a fear of heights. Is there a bypass path around it?

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: No idea.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Worth checking a guidebook or a walking forum. Many ridges have a lower path for exactly that reason.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if there isn't?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Try a smaller ridge first to see how you feel. And it's fine to turn back. Nobody good will mind.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My kids moan the whole way on every walk. Seven and nine.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Classic. Give them a job. One can be the navigator with the map, the other can be in charge of the snacks.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The snack job will start a war.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then they swap halfway. Treasure hunts work too, like spotting a feather, a red leaf or a bird nest.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: They do like collecting things.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Perfect. A small bag each for treasures, and a hot chocolate at the end gives them something to aim for.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I / tell them how far it is?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Talk in landmarks instead of miles. To the bridge, then the big rock, then the cafe. It feels much shorter.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Are expensive hiking socks really worth it? They're like fifteen quid a pair.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Honestly, yes, at least one or two good pairs. Merino wool socks stay warm when damp, wick sweat, and don't smell after a long day.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Mine smell after an hour.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then you'll notice the difference. Merino also tends to reduce blisters because your feet stay drier.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Do they wear out fast?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Faster than synthetic ones, usually. Blends with a bit of nylon last longer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Okay, I'll buy two pairs and / see how it goes.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Good plan. Wash them cool and skip the tumble dryer, they'll last much longer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: The walk I'm planning ends at a lake. I'd love to swim at the end.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Sounds lovely. Just be careful, mountain lakes are often much colder than they look, even in summer.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How cold are we talking?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It can be cold enough to make you gasp involuntarily, which is dangerous if your head goes under. Walk in slowly rather than jumping.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I was totally going to jump.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lots of people do. Let your body adjust for a minute or two first, and stay close to the shore.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Anything else?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Swim with someone, keep it short, and have warm clothes and a hot drink ready. You'll cool down more after you get out.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I work out how long a hike will take?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A rough rule is about three miles an hour on flat ground, plus an extra half hour for every thousand feet you climb.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So ten miles with two thousand feet of climbing would take how long?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Around three and a half hours of walking, then add time for breaks. I'd plan for four and a half to five.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That seems long.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Breaks, photos and lunch add up fast. It's much nicer to finish early than to rush down in the dark.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: True. Last time I / got back as the sun went down and it was stressful.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's exactly why. And add a bit extra in winter, when daylight is short.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Silly question. On a narrow path, who's supposed to step aside, the person going up or down?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Not silly. The usual etiquette is that people going downhill give way to those climbing up.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Why's that?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Climbing is harder to restart once you've stopped, and the person coming up has a narrower view of the path.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about mountain bikers?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Officially, bikes give way to walkers. In practice, a friendly step aside is often easier for everyone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And horses?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Everyone gives way to horses. Step to the downhill side if you can and say hello, it helps the horse know you're human.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How did I get sunburned on a cloudy, windy hike?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Clouds don't block much UV, and wind cools your skin so you don't feel yourself burning.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: That's sneaky.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: It really is. Higher up, the sun is also stronger than at sea level.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So sunscreen even in April.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Yes, and reapply it after a couple of hours or if you sweat a lot. Don't forget your ears and the back of your neck.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My ears are peeling right now. It's / honestly so embarrassing.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: A cap with a neck flap or a buff sorts that out next time. Until then, aloe gel will help.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What would I do if someone rolled their ankle halfway up a trail?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: First, get them sitting down and check if they can bear any weight on it at all.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Say they can, a little.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then it's probably a sprain. Keep the boot on for support, tighten the laces, and walk back slowly with poles or a shoulder to lean on.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Keep the boot on? I'd have taken it off.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: If you take it off, the swelling might stop you getting it back on. Ice and elevate once you're home.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: And if they can't walk at all?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Keep them warm and call emergency services. Give your exact location, an offline map app can show your coordinates.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My best friend uses a wheelchair and I want to plan a day out on a trail together.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Lovely idea. Many parks now have accessible trails with smooth, firm surfaces and gentle slopes.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: How do I find them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Look on the park or council website, they often list accessible routes with details on gradients, gates and toilets.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: She'd hate anything too short and boring.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Then look for old railway lines and reservoir paths. They're flat, often long, and have great views.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Should I / ask her to choose?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Definitely. She'll know what works for her chair, and you can plan the picnic.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: There are tons of blackberries along my usual trail. Is it safe to eat them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Blackberries are one of the safest wild fruits, since there's nothing toxic that looks similar.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Even ones right by the path?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Pick the ones higher up, away from where dogs might wander. Avoid bushes next to busy roads.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: What about the red berries / right next to them?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Leave those unless you're absolutely sure what they are. Some red berries are poisonous.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Got it, black and bumpy only.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Exactly. Bring a tub and you'll have a crumble by the evening.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: My son keeps telling me to track my hikes on an app. I don't see the point.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: You don't need to. But some people enjoy seeing their routes on a map and how far they've gone over a year.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: I've been walking these hills for forty years without a phone.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That's a lot of knowledge in your head. An app won't replace that.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: So what's he on about?

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: Probably safety. Some apps let you share your location live with family, so they know you're okay if you're out alone.

turns.speaker: user
turns.text: Hm. That might stop / his mother worrying, I suppose.

turns.speaker: moshi
turns.text: That might be the real reason. You could just turn it on for solo walks and ignore the rest.

option_sets.lead_in: We're planning a hike next Saturday and I have to choose the trail.
options: The first trail is a flat loop around a lake, about five miles, with lots of shade.
Then there's a steep climb to a ridge with amazing views, but it's eight miles and pretty rocky.
Option three is a forest trail along a river with a few small waterfalls, moderate and six miles.
And the last one is a coastal path that's easy but gets crowded on weekends.
moshi_comment: The river trail sounds like a great middle ground, waterfalls and a moderate distance. The ridge climb is the most rewarding if everyone is fit and has good shoes. The lake loop is best if anyone in the group is new to hiking.
How experienced is everyone in the group? If it's mixed, I'd go with the river trail. The coastal path might be too busy on a Saturday.

option_sets.lead_in: I need to pick hiking boots before my trip, and I've tried on a few pairs.
options: The first pair is heavy leather boots, super sturdy and waterproof, but they need breaking in.
The second pair is lightweight trail runners, really comfortable right away, but not waterproof.
And the third pair is mid height synthetic boots, kind of in between, with decent ankle support.
moshi_comment: For most trips, the mid height synthetic boots are a solid compromise between comfort and support. The leather boots are best for rough, wet terrain if you have time to break them in. The trail runners are great on dry, well kept trails.
What kind of terrain and weather are you expecting? If it's wet and rocky, go for the leather boots, but start wearing them now. If it's dry, the trail runners will feel amazing.

option_sets.lead_in: My old daypack is falling apart and I've narrowed the new one down, can you help me pick?
options: There's a tiny twenty litre one, super light, just enough room for water, a jacket and lunch.
Then a thirty litre pack with a proper hip belt and a mesh back so you don't get a sweaty back.
And a bigger forty litre pack that would also work for overnight trips, but it's heavier and costs more.
moshi_comment: If it's mostly day hikes, the thirty litre with the hip belt is the sweet spot. The tiny one fills up fast once you add layers, and the forty is overkill unless you really will camp.
Go for the thirty litre. The mesh back makes a real difference on warm days, and you won't miss the extra space of the big one for day trips.

option_sets.lead_in: It's my dad's seventieth and he wants a birthday walk, but I need to choose where.
options: One idea is the lighthouse loop, it's flat along the cliffs, about four miles, with a cafe at the end.
Another is the hill behind his old school, a steady climb, quite sentimental for him, about six miles.
Or there's the bluebell woods, short and gentle, but it might be muddy this time of year.
moshi_comment: The hill behind his old school has the most meaning, and six steady miles sounds doable if he still walks a lot. If he's less sure on his feet, the lighthouse loop with cake at the end is the safest bet.
I'd lean towards his old school hill, a birthday walk with memories is special. Keep the lighthouse loop as a backup if the weather turns, and skip the woods if it's been raining.

option_sets.lead_in: I've got a free Thursday and three trails in mind, I just can't pick.
options: There's the gorge walk, narrow and rocky with waterfalls, about three hours, and you need decent grip.
Then the moorland ridge, wide open views the whole way, but no shelter at all if it gets windy.
Or the old drovers' road, long and easy, mostly grassy, with a village pub roughly halfway.
moshi_comment: Check the wind first. If it's calm, the moorland ridge gives you the biggest views, and if it's wet, the gorge waterfalls will be at their best, as long as your boots grip well.
On a free weekday, the gorge will be quiet and the waterfalls make it special. The drovers' road is lovely but easy, so save it for a day when you want a pub lunch more than a challenge.

option_sets.lead_in: I need a new rain jacket before the autumn and the shop gave me three to try.
options: A really light packable shell that folds into its own pocket, but the guy said it's not great in long downpours.
A heavier three layer jacket, totally waterproof and breathable, but nearly double the price.
A cheap plastic poncho type thing that covers me and my backpack, ugly but it works.
moshi_comment: For autumn, I'd spend more on the three layer jacket. The light shell is great in summer showers, but it'll let you down in all day rain, and the poncho turns into a sail on windy ridges.

The three layer jacket is the one you'll still have in five years. If money's tight, the packable shell plus a spare jumper is fine for short walks, but I'd skip the poncho unless it's low and sheltered.
